Lessons.Title: Find the Area of Figures
ExplanationParagraphs: Find the Area of Figures: use multiplication and addition to find areas when some or all interior grid lines are missing. Split the figure into non-overlapping rectangles, identify their side lengths, multiply, then add areas using square units. The remaining unit intervals or given measurements provide the information; the apparent size of the drawing alone does not.

Warm-up — Extend Make a Ten: mentally find 109 + 4, 109 + 14, 209 + 34 and 219 + 34, in order. Make a ten or add by place value. For example, move one from 34 to 209 to make 210 + 33 = 243. Compare the first two sums and the last two: in each pair the second sum is ten greater. Explain the change in the addends, record strategies, and restate another student’s method.

Bye-Bye Squares: first inspect an outline with no lengths or squares. Record a notice, a question and what further information would help you find the area. Without a unit or measurements, the outline has no determined numerical area. Now inspect Figure 1 in the companion: some squares remain in its upper-right corner and the edges have equal unit intervals. Use them to identify the side lengths. The top rectangle is seven units by five units and the lower-right leg is three units by three units. The area is (7 × 5) + (3 × 3) = 35 + 9 = 44 square units.

For Figure 1, a different vertical split gives a four-by-five left rectangle and a three-by-eight right rectangle. Their areas are 20 and 24, again totaling 44 square units. Work with a partner, explain how the partial grid gives the side lengths, and compare both splits. If you draw in the missing squares to count, also try a method that multiplies the inferred lengths. Use a simpler figure first if that helps you explain the method.

Figure 2 is T-shaped and has only boundary unit intervals. The top bar is eight units wide and three units high. Its centered stem is two units wide and extends four units below the bar. The areas are 24 and 8, so (8 × 3) + (2 × 4) = 32 square units. Count the intervals between marks, including the end intervals; seven interior top marks define eight units. Think quietly, then compare your method with a partner. The goal is to use side lengths without rebuilding every square.

How Many Pavers Do We Need? A paver is a square stone or block used for a patio. Noah’s patio has a nine-foot top, a six-foot left side, a four-foot right side, a six-foot inside horizontal edge, a two-foot inside vertical edge, and a three-foot bottom. Each square paver is one foot by one foot, so it covers one square foot. Split the patio into a nine-by-four top rectangle and a three-by-two lower-left rectangle. Their areas are 36 ft² and 6 ft², giving 42 ft². Noah therefore needs 42 one-square-foot pavers, assuming the ideal mathematical covering in the problem without gaps or waste.

A second patio method uses a three-by-six left rectangle and a six-by-four right rectangle: 18 + 24 = 42 ft². Explain which labelled measurements each method uses and why some labels are unnecessary for that particular split. The count of pavers is 42 pavers; the area is 42 square feet. These have the same number because every paver covers exactly one square foot, but they are different quantities. The preceding T-shaped figure has area 32 square units; do not substitute its answer for Noah’s different patio.

Prepare a labelled visual display showing your split, multiplication expressions and total. Investigate other groups’ displays, compare strategies (MLR7 Compare and Connect), and explain why they yield the same area. Watch for overlapping rectangles that count some squares twice. Your teacher checks the drawing, inferred lengths, unit meanings, display and actual partner discussion; numeric answers alone cannot establish these activities.

Lesson synthesis: explain what lets you find area when a figure is not fully gridded. Imagine equal unit squares, identify rectangle side lengths, and use multiplication and addition. Explain how the partial grid, boundary intervals and finally only side-length labels each provide enough information. Reflect on whether your strategy shifted from counting to multiplying.

New Edulytics Cool-down: a separate ungridded figure has a top rectangle nine units by three units, joined to a two-by-four lower-left leg. Find its area and show a parenthesized expression. (9 × 3) + (2 × 4) = 35 square units. A vertical split gives (2 × 7) + (7 × 3) = 14 + 21 = 35. The teacher reviews the decomposition and explanation. This independently authored task does not reproduce the publisher-gated Find the Area Cool-down.

Optional centers: Five in a Row: Multiplication, stage 2 (factors 1–9), reinforces the multiplication work; Five in a Row: Addition and Subtraction, stage 8 (add within 1,000 with composing), is supporting practice. Explain how a known product helps with an unfamiliar rectangle.

KeyConcepts.Title: Infer side lengths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Partial squares and unit intervals preserve information when grid lines disappear.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Count intervals and connect them to rectangle sides.
KeyConcepts.Example: Seven interior top marks define eight unit intervals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Add non-overlapping areas
KeyConcepts.Definition: The whole is covered exactly once by its rectangle parts.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Multiply each part’s side lengths, then add the square-unit areas.
KeyConcepts.Example: The partially gridded figure covers 35+9=44 square units.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distinguish figures and quantities
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different figures can have different areas, and a tile count differs from area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use the actual figure’s dimensions and the requested unit.
KeyConcepts.Example: T-shape 32 square units; Noah 42 pavers and42 ft².

KeyConcepts.Title: Compare decompositions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Different valid splits cover the same region.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Link every product to its rectangle and explain unused measurements.
KeyConcepts.Example: For Noah,(9×4)+(3×2) and(3×6)+(6×4) both give42 ft².

WorkedExamples.Title: Partial grid
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the area of Figure 1.
WorkedExamples.Method: Read unit intervals and split horizontally.

WorkedExamples.Title: Boundary intervals
WorkedExamples.Question: Find the T-shaped Figure 2 area.
WorkedExamples.Check: Stem height4 excludes the top bar, preventing overlap.

WorkedExamples.Title: Noah’s patio
WorkedExamples.Question: Find both the number of one-square-foot pavers and the patio area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Split the patio into non-overlapping rectangles.
Steps: Each paver covers1 ft², so Noah needs42 pavers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assigning a numerical area to the opening unlabelled outline.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: No unit length or measurements have been supplied yet.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Ask what information is needed; use the subsequent partial grid or labels.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Side length counts the spaces between boundaries, including endpoints.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count unit intervals; seven interior marks on the top bar give eight units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Using the full height for both a top bar and an overlapping stem.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The top portion would be counted twice.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use only the stem height below the bar, or choose a disjoint vertical split.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 32 belongs to the different T-shaped figure.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use Noah’s labelled9×4 and3×2 parts to obtain42 ft² and42 pavers.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reporting an area in feet or a paver count in ft².
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Lengths, counts and areas are different quantities.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Write42 pavers for count and42 ft² for area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treating a correct number as a complete explanation or display.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source also requires methods, diagrams and comparing others’ strategies.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Show the non-overlapping split, labels and expressions, and ask the teacher to review the reasoning.

SummaryPoints: Find side lengths from remaining squares, intervals or labels, then multiply.
Split figures without overlap; add rectangle areas with square units.
The partially gridded figure covers44 square units; the T-shaped figure covers32.
Noah’s different patio covers42 ft² and needs42 one-square-foot pavers.
Explain how each product matches a rectangle and compare another valid method.
Teacher review is required for drawings, reasoning, displays and actual discussion.
